title: How Tea Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore tea from the plant's basics to its history, processing, preparation, and health claims. They open by sorting out common teas (green, black, oolong, white, herbal) and explain that all true teas come from the Camellia sinensis plant. The legendary origin with Emperor Shennong and the leaf in boiled water is covered, along with tea's spread through China, Japan (including the tea ceremony), Europe via the Portuguese and Dutch, the East India Company's Indian tea, tea clippers, and British tea taxes and smuggling. They then explain oxidation and how black, green, oolong, and white teas are processed, followed by macha, brewing temperatures and steep times, loose leaf versus bagged tea, iced tea's origin at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, antioxidants and the free radical theory of aging, caffeine levels, and a listener mail segment about left-handedness.
topics: brewing tea temperature and steep time

segments.title: Opening banter and tea types
segments.summary: The hosts open with small talk about their tea preferences and then reveal that green, black, oolong, and white tea all come from the same Camellia sinensis plant, with differences coming from processing.

segments.title: Legend of Emperor Shennong
segments.summary: The hosts recount the legend of Emperor Shennong, who reportedly discovered tea when leaves blew into his boiled water, while noting the story's truth is uncertain.

segments.title: Tea spreads through China and Japan
segments.summary: Tea's role in China during the Zhou and Han dynasties and its promotion in the Tang dynasty are discussed, followed by its spread to Japan through priests and the development of the Japanese tea ceremony.

segments.title: Tea arrives in Europe and the East India Company
segments.summary: Tea reaches Europe through Portuguese and Dutch trade in the East Indies, with Catherine of Braganza's influence in England. The end of the East India Company's China monopoly in 1834 led to Indian tea cultivation and the first Darjeeling auction in 1839.

segments.title: Tea clippers and British tea tax
segments.summary: After the monopoly ended, fast tea clipper ships raced from China to London. The hosts then cover the British tax on tea following the Boston Tea Party, widespread tea smuggling in the late 1700s, and the tax's repeal in 1964.

segments.title: Harvesting tea and oxidation
segments.summary: Tea is almost always harvested by hand, picking the top two leaves and bud. The hosts explain oxidation, comparing it to browning apples and withering leaves, and why it is controlled in processing.

segments.title: How black, green, and oolong tea are processed
segments.summary: The five-step black tea process (withering, rolling, oxidation, drying, sorting) is described, including Orthodox hand-rolling versus CTC machine methods. Green tea is steamed to stop oxidation, and oolong is partially oxidized and then steamed. Yellow tea is mentioned as a steaming accident.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short transition break before the hosts move on to matcha and tea preparation.

segments.title: White tea and matcha
segments.summary: White tea is picked only two days a year and was reserved for Chinese nobility. Matcha is shade-grown, ground powdered green tea, prepared by whisking, with L-theanine discussed as an amino acid that can cross the blood-brain barrier. The hosts also discuss matcha in restaurants and a colloid suspension.

segments.title: Brewing temperatures, steep times, and loose leaf vs bagged tea
segments.summary: The hosts list water temperatures and steep times for each tea type. They then compare loose leaf and bagged tea, noting that CTC-processed tea in bags forms clumps and that loose leaf may retain more beneficial oils. Iced tea's origin at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair and Southern sweet tea are also discussed.

segments.title: Health benefits, antioxidants, and caffeine
segments.summary: The hosts explain free radicals and the free radical theory of aging, describe antioxidants in tea, and summarize correlational health studies. They note that green tea has the most catechins and compare caffeine levels in tea and coffee, with a brief aside on USDA coffee guidance.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close with a call to drink tea and point listeners to the website and social channels.
